User reports that 'brew upgrade' started updating ALL casks, even ones marked 'auto_updates: true' in the Cask JSON API, calling it new default behavior that didn't used to happen.
"This sort of overly eager upgrading has caused me a lot of problems over the years. I really wish it didn't default to updating the entire world just because you want to update one package."
Maintainer mikemcquaid confirms cask auto-update skipping is intended but 'not yet rock solid' and asks users to file issues when it misbehaves.
"Hell yeah, tap trust!!!" — positive reaction to new brew tap trust feature described in docs.brew.sh/Tap-Trust.
User says they stopped using Homebrew after being 'screwed too many times on mandatory upgrades I couldn't pin,' switching to a combination of Mise and MacPorts to avoid surprise breakage.

User describes switching entire dev environment from Homebrew+pipx+npm to mise, citing zero version lag and being able to install any arbitrary package version, unlike waiting for Homebrew taps to update (citing llama.cpp tap skipping releases).

User recalls packaging a Python app for Homebrew as painful: importing ~50 dependencies as 'resources', building from source, declaring toolchains for 5 languages, hour-long CI waits, and eventually the package became unpackable due to a build-time dependency loop.
"Congrats on the performance improvements. That's the most pleasant `brew upgrade` session I've had in years."
User wishes for a standard Homebrew way to install multiple versions of node, php and Python, currently relying on pyenv/nvm alongside Homebrew.
Complaint that Homebrew's aggressive Intel deprecation is dropping support for old Mac hardware even before Apple does; user feels Homebrew should maintain Intel support longer.
User asks: "Does homebrew still do that insane thing when you want to upgrade a single package it tells you 'hold my beer' and starts installing postgres and some obscure python version?"
User requests a better rollback mechanism, having broken their home server multiple times with bad InfluxDB/Grafana updates via Homebrew; now disables cleanup to keep old versions as a workaround.
User switched back to Homebrew from Nix, citing better package support/maintenance, better macOS support, and better UX, despite missing Nix's reproducibility.
User who tried hosting a Homebrew tap found it much harder than hosting apt/yum repos, since it requires running a git server rather than just a static file host with a CDN.
"I recently switched _back_ to Homebrew from Nix... Brew has won me back" despite liking Nix's reproducibility, citing better package maintenance and UX.

Trail of Bits auditor: "the findings on Homebrew were not inconsistent with what I'd expect to find on any similarly sized userspace package manager that serves its own binary builds," referencing their security audit of Homebrew.
User switched from Homebrew to MacPorts a few years ago and 'couldn't be happier.'

Long-time user recalls choosing Homebrew over MacPorts because 'brew had and has many more packages available, brew updates versions more quickly, brew uses much more simple paths that fit my brain better, brew has a pleasing simplicity.'
Positive reaction to the new HOMEBREW_BOOTSNAP environment variable allowing Bootsnap gem use to speed up repeated brew calls: "Very nice.. Can't wait to do the numbers on this!"

Workaround for casks being force-upgraded: set HOMEBREW_NO_UPGRADE_AUTO_UPDATES_CASKS=1, which a hint mentions. The user called it a rough experience because, with HOMEBREW_NO_ENV_HINTS on, this significant breaking change can happen silently.

A user wants a cooldown before new versions ship. Their example: a uv release with ~7,000 additions went out at 10:21am and was in Homebrew by 11:46am. They asked what human review happened and said Arch Linux hadn't shipped it yet.

A user wanted to try Elixir 1.20 right after its announcement, but brew lagged behind. Installing Erlang and Elixir another way wasn't worth it in that moment. They suggested stable/edge release channels.

A user's company publishes a package on Homebrew. Its recipe points to a URL that Homebrew automation checks for new versions and bumps automatically, so no human ever updates it manually, yet the newest version is always installable.

A user moved to MacPorts because of Homebrew's aggressive support phase-out schedule; their daily-driver iMac is now in Tier 3. They "absolutely loved Homebrew" but won't buy new hardware just to keep using it.

A user switched to MacPorts because of permission issues with brew and used it for years. They switched back after MacPorts started wanting to install a huge number of packages just to install something small like wget.

A user stopped using Homebrew after being "screwed too many times on mandatory upgrades that I couldn't pin." They now use Mise and MacPorts. They also complained of waiting on Homebrew to upgrade packages (llama.cpp skips every 10 releases).

Packaging a Python app for Homebrew was painful for one user: about 50 dependencies imported as resources, build toolchains for 5 languages, over an hour of CI per update. A later build-time dependency loop made it unpackable. They moved their dev env to Mise but still use Homebrew for casks.

Homebrew has been a great way to quickly bootstrap an environment on immutable Linux distributions; Bazzite, Bluefin and Aurora bundle it by default. A Bluefin user said the Homebrew experience on Linux is great.
"Congrats on the performance improvements. That's the most pleasant `brew upgrade` session I've had in years"

Most of this user's Mac setups are based on Homebrew. They still rely on pyenv or nvm for Python and Node and wish there were a standard Homebrew way to install multiple versions of node, php and Python.
"The deprecation of Intel support is agressive!" Mac enthusiasts who use old Intel Macs as servers will lose Homebrew support a year before Apple drops them.

A user wants a rollback mechanism. Bad InfluxDB and Grafana updates broke their home server multiple times and rolling back was a huge pain. Their workaround is disabling cleanup so old package versions are kept.

A user switched back to Homebrew from Nix. Reasons: packages seem better maintained, Mac support is better (some Nix packages disable features on macOS), and the UX is better. They miss Nix's reproducibility and flakes.

After hosting apt and yum repositories, a user found hosting a Homebrew tap much harder. Your server must implement the git protocol, so you can't just put it behind a CDN; you need to run and fortify a git server.
"I use nix on both mac and linux, also on CI where homebrew is especially brittle"

On Linux, Homebrew requires pre-built executables to be installed into /home/linuxbrew. A user said this makes it basically impossible to quickly install programs with Homebrew on systems where you don't have root.
A user who switched from MacPorts to brew early on gave these reasons: brew had and has many more packages, updates versions more quickly, uses simpler paths, and "has a pleasing simplicity".

Compared to MacPorts years ago, users recalled Homebrew as easier and snappier with less friction. MacPorts was slower because it brought in its own dependencies, needed sudo more, and had fiddly parts.

Homebrew documents an unauthenticated JSON data API over its package metadata ("Homebrew Formulae JSON API Documentation": /api/formula.json, /api/cask.json, per-package and analytics endpoints) with curl examples and a full example response schema, and the manpage designates formulae.brew.sh/api as the JSON API download mirror. It is a machine-readable data API; no formal API-description artifact (OpenAPI or equivalent) exists, the endpoints carry no version segment, there is no runner (static examples), and the schema's deprecation fields govern formulae lifecycles, not the API surface.
